title: Elara Spark and the Science Fair Jinx
markdown:
Elara Spark wanted one ordinary science-fair day. She was eleven, brilliant, and jinxed in the small, inconvenient way that did not involve thunderbolts, only exploding teacups and potato batteries that chose the worst possible moment to catch fire. In the gym of Northwood Elementary, under a banner that said INNOVATION AND INGENUITY, she polished Mount Fumarole, a slightly wobbly model volcano, as if shine could bargain with fate.

Her notebook cover was a map of ink and hastily drawn disasters. She had once written, in a corner, that true talent hid in what looked like bad luck. She was about to test the sentence.

She set a tiny plastic dinosaur at the volcano’s base. Above her, a plump pigeon with no sense of occasion decided the peak was a target. SPLAT. A truly enormous white gift landed on her carefully painted striations.

“Oh, for goodness sake.” Elara dabbed. The cloth spread the goo into a glacier. The familiar prickle arrived: so much for a smooth morning. She flipped the notebook. Event 1: Avian Assault. Suspicious detail: pigeon arrived the instant I felt hopeful. Coincidence? Unlikely.

She considered the janitor’s closet until pickup. Then she saw Professor Quibble, a judge, beaming at a terrarium of perfect ferns as if ferns had invented joy. A flicker of defiance went through her.

“No,” she whispered. “Still my project.” She tied her shoelaces extra tight, a small superstition against the coming weather, and stayed. Vinegar and baking soda fizzed somewhere to her left. A paper-mâché solar system wobbled on a table that had one short leg. The gym smelled of floor polish and nerves.

Mount Fumarole was meant to erupt with harmless red colouring and a puff of dry ice. During the demonstration, static lifted the hair on her arms. Instead of vapour, the volcano WHOOSHED a storm of red glitter over Elara, the onlookers, and a neighbouring static-electricity board. The hall went briefly disco. The powder smelled of sugar and left a slick sheen.

“Incredible!” boomed Professor Quibble, brushing glitter from oversized spectacles. “A most energetic eruption. A new volcanic particulate, perhaps?”

Elara’s smile was weak and sparkly. Event 2: Glitter Bomb. Suspicious detail: static surge coincided with… a cat? She scanned. Marmalade, her ginger catastrophe, sat on a chair with unnerving calm, as if to say she had been foolish to hope. He appeared only when the jinx hit overdrive, usually with a meow that sounded like a sigh.

Parents clapped politely at a robot that waved. Someone’s baking-soda geyser went off early and was applauded anyway. Elara wiped glitter from the dinosaur’s snout and told herself the worst had already happened. Marmalade blinked, which was never a good review.

Then a rogue bouncy ball escaped the Physics of Elasticity table, ricocheted the length of the gym, kissed a fire-extinguisher, and thudded onto her display. It did not smash anything. It only nudged Mount Fumarole enough to loosen the lava-flow nozzle, which rolled toward the edge like a traitor. She caught it with both hands and a sound that was not quite a word.

While she scrambled to reseat the nozzle, the extension cord for her little breeze-fan vanished. She had plugged it in herself, twice, because jinxed children double-check. She found it later, coiled with saintly innocence behind The Wonders of Fungi, as if mushrooms had needed a breeze more than geology.

Through it all, Fenella Button kept glancing over. Her hair defied gravity. Her lab coat wore tea stains and stray wire. Her own project, a clockwork octopus of gears and lights, hummed as if it had never met a pigeon. Between glances she tightened a bolt, then loosened it, then tightened it again, which was how Fenella thought. She offered Elara a lopsided grin and a square of slightly melted chocolate, because science fairs were long and glitter was not lunch.

“Don’t worry about the ripples,” Fenella mumbled. “Biggest waves start with small splashes. Sometimes the splashes are very confused pigeons.”

Elara’s eye caught the exhibit beside hers: a flawless self-watering Venus flytrap, traps open as if waiting for a snack. In its humidity-sensor wiring, a faint flicker. The same flicker she had seen when the fan cord wandered and the static surged. Marmalade’s fur bristled.

She wrote faster. Intermittent flicker at flytrap. Power fluctuations. Connection to everything?

Ms. Stern, head judge, swept past like a storm cloud in a pressed suit. She frowned at glitter, at the leaning nozzle, at Elara. “Miss Spark. Your presentation is unconventional. One might say chaotic.”

A hush moved down the aisle: judging proper, clipboards, the smell of Ms. Stern’s peppermint. Elara squared the dinosaur. The volcano, glitter-scarred and nozzle-repaired, still stood.

The finale arrived on oversized paws. The school mascot, a fluffy badger famous for enthusiasm and poor footwork, charged in for a morale photograph and tripped on a power cord that had not been there a moment before. In a whirl of fur the badger’s flailing paw swept the volcano. Mount Fumarole did not merely fall. It cascaded. Slopes crumbled like a sandcastle at a mean tide. Paint smeared. Leftover red bled into a muddy puddle that looked like giving up. Someone gasped. Someone laughed and then stopped laughing.

Elara stared. Recognition, gone. The jinx sat on her shoulders, heavy as wet sand. A lump rose in her throat. Marmalade offered one mournful meow that did not help and was, somehow, exactly on time.

Fenella appeared without the grin, brow furrowed, eyes sharp. “They say the universe throws curveballs. What if the curveballs are guideposts? What if the misfortunes are clues?” She nodded at the notebook. “You’ve been scribbling like a detective. What have you observed?”

Elara traced the frantic lines. “The pigeon. The static. The cord. The flicker. Every time something went wrong, there was a surge. The jinx happens around the surges. Like I’m an antenna—but only when something else is already wrong.”

Fenella’s eyes widened. She pointed from the flytrap to a large humming generator in the far corner, the drone that powered most of the fair. “Not an antenna for disaster. You’re so attuned to things going wrong that you’re noticing the wiring everyone else is ignoring. Radar. Very sparkly radar.”

Ms. Stern, who had been listening with folded arms, stepped closer. She looked at the wreckage, then at the notebook. The pencil-sharp voice softened. “A faulty wire, you say?”

Elara led them past the flytrap, whose traps had closed on nothing, to the generator in the far corner. The drone was uneven if you listened the way she listened. Notebook as map, she showed the loose connection, the frayed insulation, the small problem throwing the whole hall into chaos. A spark had been waiting there like a practical joke.

The janitor arrived with the efficiency of someone who had been waiting for an excuse and a proper screwdriver. The wire was fixed. The surges stopped. Lights that had been secretly stuttering remembered how to be lights. The air settled into an honest hum.

Mount Fumarole remained a mess, a crumpled hill with one brave dinosaur. The fair, however, did not become a larger electrical story. Ms. Stern almost smiled. “Your observational skills are remarkable, Miss Spark. You have an invaluable eye for detail.”

Fenella’s octopus ticked, unbothered, and she bumped Elara’s glittery elbow. “Told you. Confused pigeons. Very scientific.”

Elara stood by the damaged volcano, notebook smudged with heroic glitter. The banner still claimed ingenuity. Marmalade curled at her feet and purred, which in his language meant well done, and also tuna, and also that the pigeon had been his idea all along.
characters: Elara Spark (capable but jinxed child hero), Marmalade (a cat that appears only to worsen suspense)
audience: children aged 11-12, fantastic story for confident middle-grade readers
